Octatonic harmony: alternating whole tones and semitones
Atonality: organised intervals without a home key
Twelve-tone writing: a row orders pitch classes
Rhythm: pulse and accent can diverge
Orchestration: register, balance and the attack of a note
Minimalism: repetition makes the change measurable
Spectralism: a timbre becomes harmonic material
A three-part plan: an exposition presents themes in two keys, a development unsettles them, and a recapitulation brings them back in the home key.
The opening section of a sonata-form movement or a fugue, where the main material is first presented, in a sonata moving to a second key.
The middle section of a sonata-form movement, where themes are broken into fragments, combined and sent through unrelated keys.
The return of the opening themes in the home key that closes the main structure of a sonata-form movement.
Italian “tail”: a closing section after the main structure has ended, sometimes only a few chords, sometimes a second development.
A form in which a main theme, the refrain, returns between contrasting episodes: A–B–A–C–A, or more.
Three sections: a first, a contrasting middle, and the first again, often decorated or altered on its return.
A form in two repeated halves: the first leaves the home key, the second returns. Baroque dances and Scarlatti’s sonatas use it.
